The whole Scrum Team collaborates to define a Sprint Goal that communicates why the Sprint is valuable to stakeholders, and the Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning
questions.explain: Both halves are Guide sentences from Topic One. The Product Owner's proposal starts the conversation and the whole Scrum Team defines the goal together, which is why the handed-down option is wrong even though it gets the proposal right. The finalization rule matters too: the Sprint Goal is settled by the end of Sprint Planning, not discovered later, because it is what the Developers then commit to and what protects the Sprint from disruptive change. The option deferring it to the Sprint Review inverts the event's purpose entirely.

questions.stem: Before starting real Sprints, a team proposes a Sprint 0 to stand up infrastructure with no usable output, plus a hardening Sprint before each release to finish testing. Which assessment is most accurate?
options: Both are standard Scrum practice when starting a new product
Neither appears in the Scrum Guide: every Sprint is a Sprint, quality does not decrease during a Sprint, and work cannot be considered part of an Increment unless it meets the Definition of Done
Sprint 0 is allowed but a hardening Sprint is not
Both are allowed provided the Product Owner agrees and stakeholders are told
questions.explain: Neither term appears in the Guide, and both contradict rules that do. Sprint 0 fails because Sprints are not phases: each one is expected to produce a usable Increment, and 'A new Sprint starts immediately after the conclusion of the previous Sprint' leaves no room for a preliminary one. A hardening Sprint fails because it is really an admission that earlier Sprints did not meet the Definition of Done, while the Guide requires that during a Sprint 'Quality does not decrease'. What is legitimate is the underlying work: infrastructure setup and testing happen inside normal Sprints, alongside something usable.

questions.stem: Why does each Scrum artifact carry a commitment?
options: To give management a contractual promise of delivery for each Sprint
To give the Scrum Master a checklist for auditing the Scrum Team
To ensure each artifact provides information that enhances transparency and focus against which progress can be measured, reinforcing empiricism and the Scrum values
To replace the need for a separate Sprint Review with stakeholders
questions.explain: That is close to verbatim: the commitments exist so each artifact provides information that enhances transparency and focus against which progress can be measured, and 'These commitments exist to reinforce empiricism and the Scrum values for the Scrum Team and their stakeholders.' The contractual-promise option is the tempting one, because the word commitment carries that meaning everywhere else in business; in Scrum a commitment is a target to measure progress against, not a delivery guarantee. That distinction is why the Sprint Goal can survive changes to the work selected to achieve it.

questions.stem: A stakeholder asks for a burndown chart and says Scrum mandates it as the way to track a Sprint. Which response is most accurate?
options: The Guide names burn-downs, burn-ups and cumulative flows as practices that exist to forecast progress, notes they are proven useful, and warns that they do not replace the importance of empiricism; none of them is required
This is correct: the burndown chart is Scrum's prescribed progress artifact
Scrum forbids forecasting practices, because only what has already happened may be used
The Scrum Master is required to produce a burndown chart for the Sprint Review
questions.explain: The Guide mentions those three practices once, in the Sprint section, purely as examples of things that exist. Nothing requires any of them and nothing forbids them either, which is what the ban option gets wrong: the Guide's line 'Only what has already happened may be used for forward-looking decision making' is a caution about complex environments, not a prohibition on charts. A Product Owner should be comfortable saying yes to a forecast while being clear about what it is: a projection from past observation, not a promise, and never a substitute for inspecting a real Increment.

questions.stem: Which TWO of the following statements about the Product Owner are supported by the Scrum Guide? Select two.
options: The Product Owner is accountable for the Developers conforming to the Definition of Done
The Product Owner is accountable for developing and explicitly communicating the Product Goal
The Product Owner must attend every Daily Scrum in order to answer the Developers' questions
Only the Product Owner has the authority to cancel the Sprint
The Product Owner is accountable for establishing Scrum as defined in the Scrum Guide
The Product Owner assigns Product Backlog items to individual Developers during Sprint Planning
questions.explain: The Product Goal statement is the first bullet of effective Product Backlog management, and the cancellation statement is one of the few true absolutes in the Guide. The Definition of Done option is the sharpest trap because quality feels like a Product Owner concern: the Guide places it with the Developers, who are accountable for 'Instilling quality by adhering to a Definition of Done' and who 'are required to conform' to it. Daily Scrum attendance is not required, since that event is for the Developers. Establishing Scrum belongs to the Scrum Master, and assigning items to individuals contradicts self-management.

questions.stem: Scrum is founded on empiricism and lean thinking. Which statement captures what the Scrum Guide means by those two ideas?
options: Empiricism means following a defined process precisely; lean thinking means removing people from the process
Empiricism means gathering complete requirements before starting; lean thinking means minimizing documentation
Empiricism means measuring team velocity; lean thinking means limiting work in progress
Empiricism asserts that knowledge comes from experience and making decisions based on what is observed; lean thinking reduces waste and focuses on the essentials
questions.explain: That is the Guide's own wording, in the first two sentences of Scrum Theory. The complete-requirements option is the one worth dwelling on, because it describes the exact opposite approach: predictive planning assumes the knowledge exists up front, while empiricism assumes it has to be produced by doing the work and observing the result. The velocity option smuggles in a term that appears nowhere in the Guide. Limiting work in progress is a genuine lean practice, and a good one, but it is not how the Guide defines lean thinking.

questions.stem: A founder acting as Ledgerline's Product Owner asks for one sentence that captures what Scrum makes her accountable for. Which is most accurate?
options: Delivering the Sprint Backlog by the date agreed with stakeholders
Maximizing the value of the product resulting from the work of the Scrum Team, and effective Product Backlog management, whether she does that work herself or delegates it
Managing the Developers and reporting their progress to the organization
Guaranteeing that every Product Backlog item selected for a Sprint is completed
questions.explain: Those are the two accountabilities the Guide gives the Product Owner, and the delegation clause is part of the definition rather than a footnote: 'The Product Owner may do the above work or may delegate the responsibility to others. Regardless, the Product Owner remains accountable.' The guarantee option is the most tempting, because founders and executives instinctively read accountability as a promise to deliver a scope; Scrum gives the Product Owner no such promise to make, since the Developers forecast what they select and the Sprint Goal, not the item list, is what the Sprint commits to. Managing the Developers is project-manager framing that self-management rules out.
